newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan to bite bullet for IMF loan.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan to bite bullet for IMF loan.

text.p: The Pakistani government said on Thursday it was taking "bold and difficult" decisions to win release of a stalled loan from the International Monetary Fund. It gave no details.

The cabinet of Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto, whose austerity measures in June touched off a crippling wave of strikes, approved a framework deal drawn up by negotiators in Washington, a government statement said.
Pakistani markets were already braced for a possible "mini-budget" aimed at persuading the IMF to release delayed instalments of a $600 million standby loan.
The government statement said the cabinet was briefed about the damage done to the economy by strikes in response to a budget packed with harsh taxes for the year from July 1996.

"The cabinet felt that in order to offset the negative impact of those strikes and other negative factors, bold and difficult decisions needed to be taken in the interest of consolidating a sustained economic growth and quickening the country's march towards meaningful progress," it said.
"However, the cabinet felt that even difficult decisions will have to be so taken as to make them as painless as possible and without jeopardising in any way Pakistan's security interests."
The reference to security interests seemed to suggest that austerity measures would not hit the armed forces, which get a big share of the budget.
Defence spending has previously been regarded as sacrosanct because of Pakistan's long-running conflict with India.

Stocks analyst Zuna Mansoor said earlier on Thursday that "It is believed that the government has been asked to impose an agriculture tax, reduce defence spending, cut non-development expenditure and bring down maximum customs duties to 55 percent."
The IMF has previously asked Pakistan to reduce its budget deficit to four percent of gross domestic product from anywhere between five and six percent in fiscal 1995/96.
IMF concern has focused on Pakistan's large current account deficit and shrinking foreign reserves, now at about $900 million, excluding gold.
The fund held up tranches of about $80 million each due in June and September amid doubts about Pakistan's implementation of agreed policies and confusion surrounding the 1996/97 budget.
It cannot disburse the delayed payments until a mission has visited Pakistan and completed a review of the economy.
Sources in the Finance Ministry said the IMF had made clear that it would not send a team to Islamabad until the government had come up with a credible and comprehensive package.
Analysts say the absence of an IMF accord could send stock prices reeling and deter foreign lenders.
Satisfying the IMF, however, could pose an acute political challenge to Bhutto's three-year-old government, already under opposition fire for alleged corruption and mismanagement.
Pakistan's big landowners, a politically dominant class known here as "feudals", have thwarted attempts since 1993 to impose an effective agricultural income tax.

Local traders and businessmen strongly opposed a general sales tax imposed on imports and manufactures in the June budget, forcing the government to make several concessions, which could now be withdrawn under IMF pressure.
The government said on Friday talks with the IMF in Washington had produced an "understanding" on main elements of economic stabilisation and structural reforms.

Thursday's cabinet was briefed on "the understanding between the IMF and Pakistan's (negotiating) economic team", the government statement said. "The cabinet approved the framework and authorised the team to conclude the arrangement."
